analysis.summary:
Case 05 presents a 55-year-old male with a three-centimeter lung mass discovered after an upper respiratory infection, complicated by intermittent dry cough and shortness of breath, whom he has chosen not to surgically address. The examination data reveals a constellation of findings consistent with profound Spleen Qi Deficiency as the constitutional foundation, with secondary Lung Qi Deficiency and early Spleen Yang Deficiency.

The tongue examination is diagnostically decisive: the enlargement with teeth marks indicates Spleen Qi deficiency causing the organ to swell with retained fluids that the weakened Spleen cannot transform; the pale-red body (rather than bright red) indicates inadequate Blood generation, which the Spleen normally produces from food essence; the white coating points toward Spleen Yang's inability to function as the metabolic fire, allowing pathogenic fluids to accumulate. Later notation of distended sublingual veins suggests chronic fluid congestion, typical in qi-deficient states. The pulse, described as deep and thready, provides critical confirmation: the deep quality indicates qi has withdrawn into the interior (interior qi deficiency), while the thready quality reflects insufficient blood and yin fluids to fill the vessels. Together, these signs paint a picture of constitutional exhaustion.

The history of upper respiratory infection followed by persistent dry cough and a lung mass reveals the natural trajectory of Spleen-Lung Qi deficiency. In TCM theory, the Spleen generates the Qi that the Lung relies upon to mount its defensive (Wei) function at the body's surface. When Spleen Qi is weak, Wei Qi cannot prevent pathogenic invasion; when the Lung Qi is weak, it cannot effectively expel what does invade. The mass likely represents phlegm (produced by Spleen Yang's failure to transform fluids) combined with unresolved pathogenic qi, compacted into a structural abnormality. The dry cough despite the white coating is a classic paradox of Spleen-Lung Deficiency: the body lacks the moisture-generating capacity to thin secretions or the qi-power to expel them, yet the white coat indicates damp pathology that should theoretically produce copious phlegm.

The patient's decision to decline surgery, while medically consequential, is diagnostically revealing in TCM terms. Fear, low confidence, and reluctance to undergo intervention are emotional and psychological markers of Kidney Yang deficiency—the deepest constitutional resource. This suggests the deficiency is not limited to Spleen and Lung, but extends to the foundational constitutional qi stored in the Kidneys. Such a patient would experience both the physical weakness (fatigue, shortness of breath) and the psychological weakness (fear, lack of fighting spirit) that accompany Kidney Yang insufficiency.

Treatment must respectfully acknowledge the severity: a qi-deficient patient with an established lung mass and declining Kidney Yang is approaching a critical constitutional state. The approach is not to aggressively attack the mass (which would further deplete an already exhausted body) but to gradually restore the Spleen-Lung-Kidney axis so the body's own regulatory mechanisms can manage the pathology. This is constitutional medicine, not oncology, but the two can coexist if the patient remains willing to support his own recovery through diet, herbs, movement, and emotional work.

key_findings.from_inquiry: Chronic dry cough post-upper respiratory infection; 3-cm lung mass, patient refused surgery; shortness of breath noted; no other major acute complaints—suggesting a chronic, indolent metabolic/constitutional decline rather than acute inflammatory disease.
key_findings.from_visual: Enlarged tongue with teeth marks (pathognomonic for Spleen Qi deficiency and fluid retention); pale-red body (Qi and Blood insufficiency, not excess heat); white coating (Spleen Yang weakness, failure to transform fluids); distended sublingual veins (chronic vascular congestion from deficiency).
key_findings.from_pulse: Deep quality = Qi has withdrawn into interior; thready quality = insufficient Blood and Yin fluids to adequately fill the vessels; overall pattern = constitutional qi and blood insufficiency with interior qi collapse.
key_findings.from_other: Age 55 and male sex are consistent with kidney-essence decline phase (8×7=56 years is the classical threshold for Kidney Qi exhaustion in males per the Yellow Emperor's Classic); refusal of surgery suggests fear and lack of fighting spirit (Kidney Yang-Heart Yang psychological markers).

analysis.pattern_rationale: The primary diagnosis of Spleen Qi Deficiency with Lung Qi Deficiency is supported by: (1) Pathognomonic tongue sign of enlargement + teeth marks = Spleen Qi deficiency with fluid retention; (2) pale-red body = Spleen's failure to generate Blood from food essence; (3) white coating = Spleen Yang deficiency permitting pathogenic fluid accumulation; (4) deep pulse = interior Qi deficiency; (5) thready pulse = Blood and Yin-fluid insufficiency secondary to Spleen's failure to produce them; (6) shortness of breath = Lung Qi deficiency (Lung governs Qi intake and distribution); (7) dry cough = Lung Yin insufficiency compounded by overall body fluid deficiency due to Spleen's transformation failure; (8) lung mass = structural manifestation of phlegm-damp and qi-stagnation in an environment where qi is too weak to prevent accumulation; (9) refusal of surgery + age 55 = Kidney Yang decline. This pattern integrates all four examinations into a coherent constitutional diagnosis.

treatment.therapeutic_principle: Supplement the Spleen and Middle, Augment the Qi, and Fortify the Lung. Secondary principle: Gently transform Phlegm-Damp without injuring the Spleen Yang further. Tertiary principle: Tonify Kidney Qi-Yang to restore foundational constitutional capacity and support the will to recover.
treatment.treatment_method: Internal medicinal decoctions (herbal formulas taken as water extracts) using Qi-supplementing herbs with Spleen-fortifying and Lung-tonifying modifications. Acupoint self-massage on key Qi-generation and Spleen-fortification points. Dietary therapy using easily-digestible, Qi-supplementing foods that do not require excessive Spleen transformation. Lifestyle modifications to preserve Qi. Psychological support to address fear and restore hope. Exercise appropriate for a qi-deficient constitution (gentle, not exhausting).

beneficial: Ginseng (红参, hong shen, Panax ginseng root)—the premier herb for Spleen and Lung Qi supplementation; provides immediate qi tonification and is especially indicated when constitutional deficiency is severe. Best taken as a slow-simmered broth or powder mixed into congee at 3-6g daily, under practitioner guidance due to its potent action.

Red dates and jujubes (红枣, hong zao, Ziziphus jujuba)—sweet, warm, and easily digested; directly supplement Spleen Qi and Blood; contain natural sugars that the weakened Spleen can process to build Qi. Use 5-8 dates daily in congee or soups.

Chinese goji berry (枸杞, gou qi, Lycium barbarum fruit)—tonifies Lung and Kidney Yin while gently supplementing Qi; particularly helpful for the dry cough and to prevent further Yin exhaustion. Use 10-15 pieces daily in soups or chewed as-is.

White mushrooms and medicinal fungi (灵芝, ling zhi, Ganoderma; 冬虫夏草, dong chong xia cao, Cordyceps)—tonify Lung Qi, enhance immune function, and support the body's natural resistance to pathogenic accumulation. Simmer 3-6g into broths 2-3 times weekly. Ganoderma is more accessible; Cordyceps are more potent but expensive.

Chicken meat (鸡肉, ji rou)—warm, easily digested, and the prototypical Qi-supplementing protein; when simmered with ginseng, red dates, and mushrooms into a restorative broth, it provides dense nutrition the weakened Spleen can process. Use 100-150g in soups 3-4 times per week.
recipes: Ginseng and Red Date Qi-Supplementing Congee: Use 6g sliced ginseng, 8 red dates (pitted), 100g short-grain rice, 1 liter water. Bring water to boil, add ginseng and dates, simmer 15 minutes, then add rice and simmer until rice breaks down into creamy congee (45-60 minutes). Consume warm, divided into two servings daily, for 2-3 weeks. This is the single most important therapeutic food for this pattern—it directly addresses Spleen-Lung Qi deficiency with easily absorbable carbohydrates and medicinal supplementation.

Lung-Tonifying Mushroom Broth: Use 50g fresh or dried shiitake mushrooms (sliced), 6g dried ganoderma (ling zhi, broken into pieces), 8 goji berries, 100g chicken breast (diced), 800ml water. Simmer ganoderma in water for 20 minutes (this extracts the medicinal compounds), add mushrooms and chicken, simmer another 30 minutes, add goji in final 5 minutes, season lightly with salt. Drink the broth and eat the solids 2-3 times per week. This addresses the cough, tonifies Lung Qi, and supports the weakened constitution through dual mushroom action.

foods_to_avoid: Cold and raw foods (冷食, 生食) including ice-water beverages, uncooked vegetables, and chilled fruits—these directly injure Spleen Yang, the metabolic fire required to warm food and extract Qi; a patient with white-coated, enlarged tongue cannot afford to suppress Spleen Yang further. All food should be eaten warm or at room temperature.

Greasy, fried, and heavily processed foods (油腻食物)—these are difficult for a weakened Spleen to transform; they create more pathogenic phlegm and block Qi circulation. This includes most fast foods, fried snacks, cream sauces, and heavily oiled dishes.

Alcohol, especially hard spirits (酒精)—depletes Qi directly, damages Spleen Yang, and generates heat and phlegm; a qi-deficient patient drinking alcohol is accelerating constitutional collapse. This includes all fermented beverages.
lifestyle: Avoid overwork and exhaustion (避免过劳)—Qi is the energy resource that your body has in limited supply; overwork depletes it faster than any food can replenish it. Establish clear work-rest boundaries. When fatigue appears, stop immediately and rest, rather than pushing through. This is not laziness but medical necessity for constitutional recovery.

Maintain regular sleep schedule with early bedtime (规律作息，早睡)—Qi and Blood are replenished during deep sleep, particularly between 21:00–23:00 (Gallbladder time) and 23:00–03:00 (Liver-Kidney time). Aim for sleep by 22:00 and 7-8 hours nightly. Avoid late nights and screen time after 20:00.

Keep warm, especially the lower back and abdomen (温阳，特别是腰腹部)—Spleen Yang needs warmth to function; cold environments or cold exposure will suppress the Spleen's ability to digest food and generate Qi. Wear warm clothing in cool weather, avoid cold air-conditioning, and avoid sitting in drafts. In winter, consider mild moxibustion (warming herb) over Qi-generating acupoints.

Eat at consistent times in regular meals (定时定量进食)—the Spleen functions best with routine; irregular eating or skipped meals force the Spleen to work harder and deplete Qi faster. Eat three modest, warm meals at consistent times daily. Avoid heavy dinners (eat lightly after 18:00) and snacking between meals, which confuses digestive signaling.
acupoints: Zusanli (足三里, ST36 Stomach 36)—Located 3 cun (one hand-width) below the knee crease (at the level of ST35/Dubi, the depression below the kneecap), one finger-breadth lateral to the anterior tibial crest (the bone ridge down the front of the shin). This is the premier acupoint for Qi supplementation and Spleen-Stomach fortification. Massage by pressing with the thumb pad using moderate pressure, making small circular motions, 100 times per leg daily, preferably in the morning. Purpose: directly tonifies Spleen-Stomach Qi, increases energy, improves appetite and digestion, supports immune function.

Sanyinjiao (三阴交, SP6 Spleen 6)—Located 3 cun above the inner ankle bone (medial malleolus), on the border of the tibia (the inner leg bone). This point where three Yin meridians meet directly supplements Spleen, Liver, and Kidney Yin. Massage with the thumb using moderate circular pressure, 50 times per leg, preferably in the evening. Purpose: tonifies Spleen Qi and Blood, regulates fluid metabolism, calms spirit (helpful for anxiety/fear about the lung condition).

Feishu (肺俞, UB13 Bladder 13)—Located on the back, 1.5 cun (one finger-breadth) lateral to the lower border of the 3rd thoracic vertebra (which aligns with the bottom of the shoulder blade when arms are folded across the chest). This is the Back-Shu point for the Lung. Use a massage tool or have a family member perform gentle circular massage with moderate pressure, 50 times daily, or apply warm moxibustion (warming moxa stick held 2-3cm above the skin for 5-10 minutes). Purpose: directly tonifies Lung Qi, alleviates cough, supports respiratory function.
exercise: Tai Chi (太极拳) or Qigong (气功) practice—20 to 30 minutes daily at a very slow, gentle pace, with emphasis on smooth flowing movements and deep abdominal breathing. This is the ideal exercise for qi-deficient constitutions because it does not exhaust the body but instead cultivates Qi accumulation. Styles such as Chen or Yang Tai Chi, or simple Eight Pieces of Brocade (Ba Duan Jin), are excellent. The key is consistency over intensity. If real Tai Chi classes are unavailable, there are many instructional videos online; the movement itself is less important than the mindfulness and flow.

Leisurely walking (散步) at an easy pace—30 minutes daily on flat ground, at a speed where conversation is easy and breathing is calm, 5-6 days per week. Avoid rushing, hills, or fast-paced hiking, which would deplete rather than build Qi. Morning walking in sunlight is particularly beneficial for supporting Yang Qi.
recommendations.emotional_care: The Spleen is injured by rumination, worry, and obsessive thinking—states your patient likely entered upon learning of the lung mass. The patient's refusal of surgery, while medically consequential, suggests deep fear and loss of will-power (Kidney Yang-Heart Yang dynamics). Emotional recovery is inseparable from physical recovery in this pattern. Consider: (1) Acceptance and meaning-making—the mass is now a fact; energy spent in regret or anger at the diagnosis is wasted. Help the patient reframe the focus toward what can be controlled: daily practice of tonifying herbs, movement, and acupoint massage. (2) Restoration of hope—qi-deficient patients tend toward pessimism and giving up. Frequent gentle reminders that constitutional recovery takes 3-6 months but is achievable, and that quality of life improvements (less cough, more energy, better breathing) come before any potential reversal of the mass. (3) Mind-body integration—gentle meditation or guided visualization where the patient imagines Qi flowing smoothly from food through the Spleen to the Lungs, expelling the old infection. (4) Social support—isolation worsens Spleen Qi deficiency; regular, unhurried time with family or friends supports emotional recovery. (5) Avoid harsh self-judgment—the diagnosis is not the patient's fault; deficiency develops over decades and does not indicate personal weakness.

herbal_formulas.name: Supplement the Middle and Augment the Qi (Bu Zhong Yi Qi Tang)
ingredients: Astragalus (黄芪, huang qi, Astragalus membranaceus root) 12g
Ginseng (人参, ren shen, Panax ginseng root) 6g
White Atractylodes (白术, bai zhu, Atractylodes macrocephala rhizome) 6g
Honey-fried Licorice (炙甘草, zhi gan cao, Glycyrrhiza uralensis root) 3g
Chinese Angelica (当归, dang gui, Angelica sinensis root) 4g
Tangerine Peel (陈皮, chen pi, Citrus reticulata pericarp) 3g
Bupleurum (柴胡, chai hu, Bupleurum falcatum root) 3g
Cimicifuga (升麻, sheng ma, Cimicifuga foetida rhizome) 2g
herbal_formulas.dosage: Combine all herbs by weight; decoct (simmer) in water for 40 minutes, strain, divide into two portions (morning and evening), take on an empty stomach or 1 hour before meals. One course = 14 days of daily decoction. After 2 weeks, reassess with a TCM practitioner and decide whether to continue or modify based on response. Typically 2-3 courses (4-6 weeks) are needed for noticeable constitutional improvement.
herbal_formulas.purpose: This classical formula directly addresses Spleen-Stomach Qi deficiency with a settling or sinking tendency (which manifests as shortness of breath, fatigue, and reduced organ function). It supplements the Middle Burner (Spleen-Stomach system), augments Qi throughout the body, and gently lifts Qi back toward the chest and head. The high dose of Astragalus (huang qi) tonifies Wei Qi (defensive Qi) and immune function, addressing the patient's inability to resist pathogenic accumulation. This formula is the foundation of treatment for this pattern.

herbal_formulas.name: Six Gentlemen Decoction with Lung Modifications (Liu Jun Zi Tang jia wei)
ingredients: Ginseng (人参, ren shen, Panax ginseng root) 6g
White Atractylodes (白术, bai zhu, Atractylodes macrocephala rhizome) 6g
Poria (茯苓, fu ling, Poria cocos sclerotium) 6g
Honey-fried Licorice (炙甘草, zhi gan cao, Glycyrrhiza uralensis root) 3g
Pinellia (半夏, ban xia, Pinellia ternata tuber) 6g
Tangerine Peel (陈皮, chen pi, Citrus reticulata pericarp) 3g
Lily Bulb (百合, bai he, Lilium brownii bulb) 9g—*added for Lung yin and cough*
Ophiopogon (麦冬, mai dong, Ophiopogon japonicus tuber) 6g—*added to moisten Lung and clear cough*
Luo Han Guo (罗汉果, Siraitia grosvenorii fruit) 1 piece—*added to clear Lung heat and moisten dryness*
herbal_formulas.dosage: Combine all herbs; decoct for 40 minutes, strain, divide into two portions, take with meals twice daily. One course = 14 days. Use this formula if the cough and shortness of breath are the primary bothersome symptoms. Can alternate with Bu Zhong Yi Qi Tang on a weekly basis (one week of each formula) to address both the constitutional deficiency and the respiratory symptoms simultaneously.
herbal_formulas.purpose: The classical Six Gentlemen formula supplements Spleen Qi and transforms Phlegm-Damp (critical because the white coating indicates pathogenic fluid accumulation). The added Lung-tonifying herbs (Lily, Ophiopogon, Luo Han Guo) directly moisten the Lung, clear any residual heat from the old infection, and facilitate smooth cough-expulsion. This formula addresses the cough and dry respiratory symptoms while maintaining gentle Spleen support. Use this when the respiratory complaint is most troublesome; return to the Qi-supplementing formula as the cough resolves.

warning_signs: Rapid worsening of shortness of breath, especially at rest or during minimal activity—may indicate mass growth, fluid accumulation, or cardiovascular involvement; requires immediate chest imaging and medical evaluation.
Coughing up blood or blood-tinged sputum (hemoptysis)—suggests tumor erosion, infection, or vascular involvement; requires urgent medical imaging.
Chest pain, pressure, or tightness—may indicate heart involvement, pleural inflammation, or mass-related pressure; seek immediate medical evaluation.

Fever (temperature >38.5°C / 101.3°F)—suggests possible infection (pneumonia, etc.) which could be life-threatening in a qi-deficient patient with compromised immunity; requires antibiotic evaluation.
Sudden severe fatigue or collapse—may indicate acute qi exhaustion, infection, or hemorrhage; requires emergency evaluation.
Rapid or irregular heartbeat, palpitations with dizziness—may indicate heart strain or fluid-related complications; requires cardiac evaluation.
Sudden severe swelling of the legs or face—may indicate vascular obstruction or metastatic spread; requires imaging.
contraindications: Do NOT use harsh purgative herbs (such as Da Huang/rhubarb, Mang Xiao/Glauber's salt) or aggressive heat-clearing formulas—these will further deplete the already-exhausted Spleen Qi and accelerate constitutional collapse.
Do NOT attempt aggressive phlegm-transforming or damp-draining herbs without Spleen Qi supplementation—any attack on the phlegm without first building Qi will fail and may harm the Spleen.
Do NOT use cold herbs or eat cold foods—Spleen Yang is already weak; cold exposure will shut down digestion and qi-generation.
Do NOT undergo strenuous exercise, heavy lifting, or exhausting labor—constitutional Qi is limited and must be preserved for healing, not spent on exertion.
Do NOT skip meals or practice fasting—intermittent eating further stresses the already-weakened Spleen; regular meals are mandatory for Qi restoration.

Do NOT use mineral supplements, vitamins, or heavy proteins (like beef) without food—the deficient Spleen cannot process them without support from easily-digestible carrier foods like congee or broth.
Do NOT drink alcohol in any form—alcohol depletes Qi and damages Spleen Yang; this is a hard contraindication in this pattern.
precautions.special_notes: This patient has a diagnosed lung mass and has declined surgical intervention. TCM treatment is complementary and cannot replace conventional medical monitoring. The patient MUST continue regular imaging (CT or chest X-ray) at intervals recommended by the oncology team to assess any changes in the mass. This diagnosis and treatment are aimed at improving quality of life (reducing cough and shortness of breath, increasing energy), supporting constitutional resilience, and potentially slowing progression—NOT at replacing medical care or promising cure. The deficiency pattern is chronic and recovery will be slow (3-6 months minimum before substantial improvement). Discourage the patient from expecting rapid results or from abandoning conventional medical monitoring in favor of herbs alone. The most likely beneficial outcomes are: (1) reduced cough and improved breathing within 4-8 weeks; (2) increased energy and appetite within 2-4 weeks; (3) stabilization of the mass (preventing rapid growth) with sustained herbal use; (4) improved psychological state as fatigue decreases and hope is restored. Equally important: at age 55, the patient is in a critical window for addressing constitutional decline before it becomes irreversible. Commitment to 3-6 months of consistent herbal therapy, acupoint massage, dietary change, and gentle movement is essential for meaningful results.

follow_up.timeline: Reassess in 2-3 weeks with a TCM practitioner (or at minimum every 4 weeks if geographic distance is a factor). Request a re-examination of the tongue and pulse to track objective changes.
follow_up.expected_improvement: Week 1-2: Appetite may improve; fatigue may slightly decrease. Week 2-4: Cough should diminish in frequency and intensity; shortness of breath on exertion may improve. Week 4-8: Throat should feel less dry; energy should noticeably increase; Qi restoration effects compound. Week 8-12: Significant improvement in daily function; reduced symptoms; patient should report feeling 'stronger' and 'more resilient'. Tongue should show gradual reduction in size and coating thinning. Pulse should gradually become less thready and less deep (more bouncy/strong). These improvements validate that the constitutional deficiency is being addressed and justify continuing therapy.
follow_up.next_steps: 1. Begin with Bu Zhong Yi Qi Tang for 2 weeks as the constitutional foundation. 2. If cough is severe, add Six Gentlemen with Lung modifications in week 3-4. 3. Begin acupoint self-massage immediately (does not wait for herbal decoction to arrive). 4. Implement dietary changes immediately—begin Ginseng and Red Date Congee daily. 5. At 2-week mark, report back on: cough severity (0-10 scale), shortness of breath on exertion (0-10 scale), energy level (0-10 scale), appetite (improved/same/worse). 6. At 4-week mark, arrange imaging (per oncology team schedule) and compare to prior baseline to assess any mass progression or stability. 7. Continue herbs for minimum 8-12 weeks before any major changes; deficiency recovery requires sustained effort. 8. After 8 weeks, if good progress, may reduce frequency of herbal decoction to 5-6 days per week and extend therapy for an additional 2-3 months. 9. Coordinate with any medical oncology team—inform them that herbal supplementation is occurring (they need to know for drug interactions and overall care coordination, though interaction risk is low with Qi-supplementing herbs).

parsed.disclaimer: Traditional Chinese Medicine is a complementary healthcare system and should not replace conventional medical care. This TCM diagnosis and treatment recommendations are intended to support quality of life and constitutional recovery in addition to, not instead of, medical oncology care. The patient has a diagnosed lung mass and must continue regular imaging surveillance and medical monitoring as recommended by the oncology team. TCM cannot cure cancer and makes no promise to reverse, shrink, or stop progression of malignant disease. The herbal formulas, acupoint massage, dietary recommendations, and lifestyle modifications described here are aimed at strengthening the body's constitutional resilience, reducing symptomatic distress (cough, shortness of breath, fatigue), and supporting the body's natural regulatory mechanisms—goals that are compatible with but secondary to medical management. Any worsening of respiratory symptoms, appearance of new symptoms, or findings on imaging that suggest rapid progression require immediate medical consultation and should not be delayed for continued herbal therapy alone. The patient should remain under the care of a licensed physician and should inform all providers (TCM and conventional) of treatments received and any supplements being taken.
